Judy Van Wyck, Chairperson Africana Studies supports the Department of Sociology in their proposal for a Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities Minor.
The AAF Faculty have several concerns that can be summarized in the following statement.
While we support a minor in social justi ce, we believe the present state of Africana Studies reflects the results of systematic lack of support, marginalization and institutionalized neglect.

Without the adequate funding, staffing and support that is necessary for any area of study to carry out basic administrative and academic functions, successful and progressive development is impeded.
Complexly, Africana Studies has "partnered" in the past with other departments in well-meaning projects.
Often the result has been that the other departments receive the recognition and subsequent funding while Africana Studies remains perpetually without recognition of its contributions and thereby unable to garner the funding and support necessary for progress.
We have seen this pattern repeated too many times and we are hoping that these kinds of institutional blocks to true equity and social justice can be dismantled.
We would like our support of the Social Justice and Civic Responsiblities minor to strengthen increased support of Africana Studies, specifically, adequate funding, staffing and departmental status.

Toward that end, we conditionally support Sociology in the effort to establish a very important minor, the Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities minor, and even expect our relationship with Sociology to model social justice by noting the following concerns: A.) This Minor should not be seen as a segue away from the Africana Studies Major/Minor, but rather a field of study that is compatible with the academic goals of Africana Studies.
B.) Africana Studies will be able to "count" involvement in the Social Justice minor as credit in our overall assessment C.) Africana Studies maintains rightful decision -making over hiring of Faculty (especially adjunct Faculty) to teach the courses that are solely designated as AAF.
D.) The Sociology Department will keep Africana Studies informed of decisions about the minor that will impact Africana Studies.

Senate officers have heard inquiries and concerns about that move and it appears that a process improvement should be implemented that might ensure program directors are not left out of these decisions.

There were questions about the origins of such proposals and why the system is built in such a way that deans can leapfrog relevant faculty.
Beyond the mechanics of Kuali proposals, there seems to be a need to develop a better model for how interdisciplinary programs are housed at the university.
Pres.

shared information about the disparate operations of the colleges will help make a case for a By-laws mandate or other common governance structure requirements. iii.
Chapter 8 amendments related to 7 & 14 week calendar alignment - VP Preisser provided a synopsis of the plan to roll out a four program pilot of concurrent enrollment options in Fall, 2027.
The affected colleges will need to vote in favor of the plan in order for it to go forward.
The pilot will be subject to review and renewal at the end of four years.
If the Senate elects to reject renewal, the concurrent enrollments will end at the conclusion of the spring, 2031 term.
If the senate determines that the system is working well, the initiative could be expanded.
Questions were asked about the basis for renewal and if expectations can and will be set for a meaningful evaluation.
There was also a concern about institutional memory given that senators sitting at roll-out will cycle off the senate prior to the renewal phase.
VP Preisser noted that it will be up to the programs themselves to initiate their renewal so the senate will not need to ‘remember’ to do it.

A final draft is expected today and FSEC agreed to forward it to TAAC, CBUM and the ACC for review.
The legislation will be introduced in February and docketed for action in March, if ready. iv.
Clarifying and specifying launch date for SGO and 4+ attempt legislation - Staff is preparing amendments to FSEC Bills 4 and 5 to include the effective dates (Fall 2026) and will ensure that future bills all include an effective date. v.
Approval of academic calendars 8 years in advance - The Graduate School has expressed a need to set the calendar eight years in advance and such a change would require amending Sec. 8.70.10 of the UM, which prescribes a 6-year calendar.
This move would temporarily add to the workload of the ACC, which would be tasked with preparing and presenting for approval two additional calendars all in one year.
The Committee is responsible for setting the Summer, Online, standard academic year calendars, including J-term, but would need to close the gap between the 6- and 8- years out versions.
The amendment itself is straightforward and could be introduced in February. vi.

Adjusting due date for final grades - There are concerns about the timelines associated with faculty entering final grades after exams, academic standing notifications being generated, and students having adequate time to react to those notifications, especially if they need to file a grade appeal or are facing a negative finding regarding their academic standing.
URI faculty often benefit from ample time to report grades, but sometimes face quicker turnarounds.
The administration recently suggested running an AI model to determine a standard that might be optimal for students,faculty, and advising staff.
FSEC members suggested that no such effort is likely necessary, because a quick look at the due dates for the last four years reveals that faculty have not faced a deadline earlier than six days post-exam.
It would be simple and probably agreeable to simply establish that time frame as a standard.
There was some concern about the fall semester in particular, since the deadline could bump up against the Christmas holiday.
Pres.

Williams revealed that Fannon Institute Director Kim Stack has done some research on this matter and found that at most peer institutions, the norm for grade posting is 72 hours after the exam is completed.
It will be important to emphasize that the time of the staff involved in generating the standing reports is valuable too, and a balance needs to be struck between faculty preferences and the needs of staff to generate adequate and timely reports that serve students’ needs. 2
